name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: No specific public positions on early childhood education, pre-K, or Head Start were found in 2025-2026. Hagerty's support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB) in July 2025 included quadrupling the employer-provided childcare credit, which represents his primary legislative action touching childcare access, but no floor statements or press releases addressing pre-K or Head Start programs specifically were identified.
early_childhood_ed.details: Research through May 2026 found no Senate floor statements, committee testimony, or press releases from Sen. Hagerty specifically addressing early childhood education, Head Start, or pre-K funding. His legislative record on childcare-adjacent issues in this period is anchored to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 2025), which quadrupled the maximum employer-provided childcare credit and added additional relief for small businesses providing childcare benefits — framing childcare as a market-based, employer-driven issue rather than a publicly funded early education matter. No new independent early childhood education positions emerged beyond what the OBBB provision implies. His prior voting record includes opposition to the 2021 Build Back Better Act, which had contained significant universal pre-K and childcare funding provisions.

child_hunger.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which cut federal SNAP funding by an estimated $300 billion over a decade by shifting 75% of administrative costs to states, expanding work requirements to age 64, and tying state benefit cost-sharing to error rates. Tennessee advocacy groups held protests outside Hagerty's Nashville office opposing these cuts, which put 600,000 Tennessee SNAP recipients — two-thirds of whom are in households with children — at risk.
child_hunger.details: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Hagerty supported and which was signed into law in July 2025, made sweeping changes to SNAP. States previously split administrative costs 50-50 with the federal government; under the new law, states must cover 75% of administrative costs starting October 2026 and an escalating share of benefit costs beginning in 2027 tied to payment error rates. Tennessee, with a 9.7% error rate, faces potential responsibility for 10% of its $800 million annual SNAP benefit bill. The Tennessee Commission on Children and Youth estimated it would cost the state an additional $110 million annually just to preserve benefits for children. SNAP work requirements were also extended to age 64 and now apply to parents of children 14 and older. Safety net organizations demonstrated outside Hagerty's Nashville office during the Senate consideration of the bill.

parental_support.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which raised the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200 per child, made it permanent, and indexed it to inflation. The same legislation also strengthened the paid family and medical leave credit and quadrupled the employer-provided childcare credit. These provisions represent Hagerty's affirmative parental support record in 2025-2026.
parental_support.details: When the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in July 2025, Hagerty was among the Tennessee delegation praised for supporting the Child Tax Credit expansion. The CTC increase to $2,200 per child was notable given it had been set to expire in 2025, and the permanent indexing to inflation addressed a long-standing criticism of the original 2017 TCJA credit. The legislation also made the adoption tax credit partially refundable up to $5,000 and indexed it for inflation. The OBBB also quadrupled the maximum employer-provided childcare credit (up to $500,000; $600,000 for small businesses) and strengthened the paid family and medical leave credit — framed as market-based mechanisms rather than direct public programs. No standalone paid family leave bills were introduced by Hagerty in 2025-2026.

name: Marquita Bradshaw
bio: Memphis environmental justice activist who won the 2020 Democratic primary against expectations. Running again on environmental and economic-justice platform.
photo_credit: Bradshaw for Senate official campaign website

early_childhood_ed.summary: Bradshaw supports universal pre-K education and quality childcare as part of a broader platform calling for funding public education at levels comparable to military spending. These positions, first articulated during her 2020 campaign and reaffirmed on her current 2026 campaign website, represent her most recent public stance; no new 2025-2026 specific statements on early childhood education were found.
early_childhood_ed.details: Bradshaw's campaign website at marquitabradshaw.com consistently reflects support for universal pre-K, quality childcare, and high-quality public education from pre-K through grade 12. Her signature framing — 'I am a lifelong proponent of funding our education system the same as we do our military' — appears on her current issues page. Her 2020 platform explicitly listed 'Fund universal pre-K education' and 'Provide quality childcare.' As a single working-class mother who raised her son in Memphis, she has drawn personal connections between access to childcare and economic opportunity. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign announcements specifically addressing Head Start funding levels or childcare cost legislation were found.

child_hunger.summary: No specific 2025-2026 public statements from Bradshaw on child hunger, SNAP, Summer EBT, or school nutrition programs were found. Her broader platform emphasizes working-class economic justice and healthcare access, but she has not issued candidate statements addressing Tennessee's Summer EBT opt-out controversy or the SNAP cuts enacted through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
child_hunger.details: Research through May 2026 found no press releases, social media posts, or campaign statements from Marquita Bradshaw specifically addressing SNAP, Summer EBT, child hunger, or school nutrition programs. This is notable given the significant Tennessee-specific child hunger debate: Governor Lee's decision to opt out of the $84 million federal Summer EBT program (affecting roughly 700,000 children), the OBBB's $300 billion SNAP cut package, and bipartisan state-level pushback including HB 1835 to restore Summer EBT participation. Bradshaw's OnTheIssues Families & Children page shows no stance on record.

parental_support.summary: Bradshaw supports a $15 minimum wage, healthcare for all, and high-quality public education as her core economic support mechanisms for working families. No specific positions on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or direct childcare cost programs were found in 2025-2026 research.
parental_support.details: Bradshaw's current campaign issues page calls for 'fully and aggressively fighting for the federal recognition and implementation of a living wage beginning at immediately increasing the minimum wage to $15.00 an hour.' Her 2020 platform included 'relieve current student debt, provide quality childcare' as part of her economic agenda. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign statements addressing the OBBB's child tax credit provisions, federal paid leave legislation, or childcare affordability were found. OnTheIssues records no stance from Bradshaw on the child tax credit, paid family leave, or childcare cost subsidy programs.
